definition: A DNS record mapping a name to an IPv4 address.
A DNS record mapping a name to an IPv6 address.
An acknowledgement: a TCP packet field telling the sender which bytes have arrived.
A redundancy setup where all nodes serve traffic at once and share the load.
A redundancy setup where one node serves traffic and a standby takes over only if it fails.
Announcing the same IP address from many locations so the network routes each user to the nearest one.
The server that holds a domain's actual records and gives the final answer.
Automatically adding or removing instances based on a metric such as CPU, request rate or queue depth.
The fraction of time a service works correctly, often written in nines (99.9% is three nines).
Quick arithmetic with round numbers to get an answer within a small factor, used to size a design before building it.
Link bandwidth × round-trip time: how much data must be in flight, unacknowledged, to keep a link fully busy.
The HTTP header that tells browsers and caches whether, and for how long, a response may be stored and reused.
A signed document binding a domain name to a public key, issued by a certificate authority.
An organisation trusted by browsers and operating systems to sign certificates after checking who controls a domain.
The sequence from a site's certificate through intermediates up to a trusted root, each signed by the next.
The named set of algorithms a TLS connection uses for key exchange, encryption and integrity.
A program that starts a request: a browser, a mobile app, another service or a scheduled job.
A DNS record that makes one name an alias for another name.
A request with If-None-Match or If-Modified-Since that returns 304 Not Modified, with no body, if the cached copy is still current.
Algorithms (slow start, CUBIC, BBR) that limit how fast TCP sends so it does not overload the network between hosts.
An HTTP request with an Upgrade header asking the server to switch the connection to another protocol, such as WebSocket.
Mapping keys and servers onto a ring so adding or removing a server moves only a small share of keys.
The observation that systems tend to mirror the communication structure of the organisation that builds them.
A self-contained packet sent without a connection; UDP's unit of data.
Daily active users: the number of distinct users who use the product on a given day.
A method for two parties to agree on a shared secret over a public channel without an eavesdropper being able to compute it.
Services that must be deployed together or share a database: the costs of microservices without their independence.
The Domain Name System: the distributed directory that turns names like example.com into IP addresses.
Data leaving a system or network, such as responses and downloads. Cloud providers usually charge for it.
An open-source L7 proxy built for service-to-service traffic, commonly used as a sidecar in service meshes.
A version tag a server attaches to a response so a client can later ask 'has this changed?' cheaply.
One request triggering many parallel sub-requests, often waiting for all of them to answer.
The effect where rare slow responses on each backend become common for requests that wait on many backends.
Preventing a fast sender from overwhelming a slow receiver; in TCP the receiver advertises how much buffer space it has.
A server in front of clients that sends their requests out to the internet on their behalf.
A property where per-session keys mean a long-term private key stolen later cannot decrypt previously recorded traffic.
Both sides can send at the same time, independently.
DNS that returns different answers depending on where the resolver appears to be, steering users to a nearby region.
Data flows in only one direction at a time; SSE is effectively one-way, server to client.
When one lost or slow item at the front of a queue holds up everything behind it.
A periodic probe a load balancer sends to each backend to decide whether it should receive traffic.
A small periodic message (ping) sent to prove a connection or node is still alive.
Adding capacity by running more machines or copies of a service, rather than making one machine bigger.
Hypertext Transfer Protocol: the request–response protocol of the web, with methods, headers, status codes and bodies.
A property of an operation where doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once, which makes retries safe.
An HTTP method where repeating the same request has the same effect as sending it once, such as PUT or DELETE.
A signed token that carries claims such as a user id and expiry, so servers can verify it without a lookup. Hard to revoke before it expires.
Reusing one TCP connection for several HTTP requests instead of opening a new one each time.
Balancing on IP addresses and ports at the transport layer, without reading the HTTP request.
Balancing on application data such as the URL path, headers or cookies, which requires parsing HTTP.
How long one operation takes from start to finish, measured in time per request.
A balancing method that sends each new request to the server with the fewest active connections.
L = λW: the average number of items in a stable system equals the arrival rate times the average time each spends inside.
A component that receives requests and spreads them across several backend servers, skipping servers that fail health checks.
The client sends a request and the server holds it open until there is data or a timeout, then the client asks again.
A separately deployable service that owns one business capability and its data, and talks to other services over the network.
A single deployable whose modules own their own code and data and only call each other through defined interfaces.
An application built and deployed as one unit. It can still run as many identical copies behind a load balancer.
Mutual TLS: both client and server present certificates, so each proves its identity to the other.
Carrying many independent streams over one connection at once, as HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 do.
A widely used event-driven web server and reverse proxy.
A DNS record naming the authoritative nameservers for a domain.
How many times higher the busiest period's traffic is than the average, typically 2–10×.
The value below which a given share of measurements fall; p99 latency is the time 99% of requests are at or under.
A balancing method that picks two backends at random and sends the request to the less busy one; nearly as good as checking every backend.
The secret half of a key pair; it signs data or decrypts what the public key encrypted, and must never leave the owner.
The half of a key pair that can be shared; it encrypts data or verifies signatures made by the private key.
Queries (or requests) per second, the standard unit for load on a service.
A transport protocol over UDP, with built-in TLS 1.3 and independent streams, that HTTP/3 runs on.
How many reads a system serves for each write; it decides whether to optimise for reads (caches, replicas) or writes.
The DNS server (often your ISP's, or 8.8.8.8 or 1.1.1.1) that chases a lookup through root, TLD and authoritative servers and caches the answer.
A guarantee that every byte arrives, in order, by retransmitting anything not acknowledged.
A copy of a database that receives changes from a leader; read replicas serve read queries.
The pattern where a client sends one request and waits for one response from the server.
A proxy reading the whole backend response quickly, freeing the backend, then feeding it to a slow client itself.
A server in front of your backends that receives client requests on their behalf and forwards them.
The top of the DNS hierarchy; it points resolvers to the right top-level-domain servers.
A balancing method that sends each new request to the next server in a fixed rotation.
An HTTP method that should not change server state, such as GET or HEAD.
A counter on every TCP segment that marks its position in the byte stream, so the receiver can reorder and detect gaps.
A program that waits for requests and answers them. One process can be a server to some callers and a client of others.
A browser standard where the server streams text events over one long-lived HTTP response, with automatic reconnect.
A layer of sidecar proxies plus a control plane that handles service-to-service routing, retries, mTLS and telemetry.
Data that ties a series of requests to one user, such as login status or a cart, usually found by a session id in a cookie.
Splitting one dataset's rows across several databases by a key, so each database holds a slice.
The client asks the server for updates on a fixed timer; the server answers at once, usually with nothing.
A proxy process deployed next to each service instance that handles its network traffic.
A component whose failure takes the whole system down because nothing else can take over (SPOF).
The amount of unacknowledged data a sender may have in flight; it slides forward as ACKs arrive.
Secure Sockets Layer, TLS's deprecated predecessor; the name survives in everyday speech.
A server that keeps data between requests in its own memory or disk, so some requests must reach that specific server.
A server that keeps no request-to-request data in its own memory or disk, so any copy can handle any request.
A three-digit number in an HTTP response stating the result, grouped 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.
A long-lived connection that stays bound to one server for its whole life, so it cannot be moved without reconnecting.
Load balancer routing that sends each user back to the same server, usually because their session lives in that server's memory.
Replacing an old system gradually by routing one capability at a time to new code until the old code can be deleted.
The small DNS client in your operating system that forwards lookups to a recursive resolver.
The 'synchronise' flag on the first TCP packet, which asks to open a connection and carries the starting sequence number.
The latency of the slowest requests, usually p99 and above.
Transmission Control Protocol: a connection-based transport that delivers a reliable, ordered byte stream between two hosts.
The SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK exchange that opens a TCP connection; it costs one round trip before data can flow.
How many operations complete per unit of time, such as requests per second.
A server for a top-level domain such as .com that points to each domain's authoritative nameservers.
Transport Layer Security: the protocol that encrypts and authenticates traffic, the 'S' in HTTPS.
The opening exchange where client and server agree on algorithms, verify the certificate and derive shared session keys.
Letting a proxy do TLS encryption and decryption so backend servers do not have to.
Decrypting TLS at a proxy or load balancer, which then forwards plain or re-encrypted traffic to backends.
Time to live: how many seconds a DNS answer may be cached before it must be looked up again.
A set of guidelines for building cloud services, written at Heroku; factor VI says app processes should be stateless and share nothing.
A DNS record holding free text, used for domain verification and email security such as SPF.
User Datagram Protocol: a connectionless transport that sends independent packets with no delivery, ordering or retransmission guarantees.
The fraction of time a resource is busy. Queueing delay grows sharply as it approaches 100%.
Scaling up: giving one machine more CPU, memory, disk or network capacity.
An IP address not tied to one machine, which can move to a standby when the active node fails.
A protocol, started by an HTTP upgrade, that keeps one TCP connection open for two-way messages in small frames.
Round robin where bigger servers get proportionally more turns.
